claim: Nearly one third of all human malignancies are driven by mutational activation of one of the three RAS isoforms: KRAS, NRAS and HRAS.
source: Nearly one third of all human malignancies are driven by mutational activation of one of the three RAS isoforms: KRAS, NRAS and HRAS (Roberts and Der, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roberts and Der, 2007

claim: The three major cancer types in which RAS mutations are the most prevalent are pancreatic, lung, and colorectal cancers.
source: The three major cancer types in which RAS mutations are the most prevalent (pancreatic, lung, and colorectal) all arise from epithelial tissue (Stephen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stephen et al., 2014

claim: Pancreatic, lung, and colorectal cancers all arise from epithelial tissue.
source: The three major cancer types in which RAS mutations are the most prevalent (pancreatic, lung, and colorectal) all arise from epithelial tissue (Stephen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stephen et al., 2014

claim: MCF10A cells stably transduced with oncogenic KRASG12V undergo increased proliferation.
source: Importantly, MCF10A cells stably transduced with oncogenic KRASG12V undergo numerous phenotypic changes characteristic of malignant transformation, including increased proliferation and significant loss of cell adhesion (Stolze et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stolze et al., 2015

claim: MCF10A cells stably transduced with oncogenic KRASG12V undergo significant loss of cell adhesion.
source: Importantly, MCF10A cells stably transduced with oncogenic KRASG12V undergo numerous phenotypic changes characteristic of malignant transformation, including increased proliferation and significant loss of cell adhesion (Stolze et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stolze et al., 2015

claim: Greater than 90% of surface proteins contain Asn-linked glycosylation.
source: This is advantageous because greater than 90% of surface proteins contain Asn-linked glycosylation (Schiess et al., 2009; Wollscheid et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schiess et al., 2009 and Wollscheid et al., 2009

claim: A total of 2943 tryptic peptides from approximately 500 proteins were identified in both MCF10A cells with and without KRASG12V.
source: We identified a total of 2943 tryptic peptides from ~500 proteins common in both the MCF10A cells with and without KRASG12V (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Of 2943 tryptic peptides, 1460 contained the deamidated asparagine mass shift generated by N-glycanase treatment.
source: Of 2943 tryptic peptides, 1460 contained the deamidated asparagine mass (0.984 Da) shift generated by N-glycanase treatment, providing high confidence it contained an asparagine-linked modification.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis

claim: 258 membrane-associated proteins were identified in both light and heavy samples after bioinformatic filtering.
source: Lastly, the data were filtered bioinformatically to isolate proteins annotated in UniProt to be localized to the cell surface, resulting in 1257 high confidence peptides originating from 258 membrane-associated proteins found in both light and heavy samples.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis

claim: Biological replicates showed 88% overlap in the common membrane proteins identified.
source: Biological replicates showed 88% overlap in the common membrane proteins identified, and good correlation in terms of SILAC ratios (R2 = 0.7676) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C

claim: Biological replicates showed good correlation in terms of SILAC ratios (R2 = 0.7676).
source: Biological replicates showed 88% overlap in the common membrane proteins identified, and good correlation in terms of SILAC ratios (R2 = 0.7676) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C

claim: 17 proteins were significantly upregulated by oncogenic KRASG12V.
source: In total, we identified 17 proteins that were significantly upregulated, and 22 that were significantly downregulated (fold-change >±1.75; p-value<0.01) (Figure 1B; The full dataset can be found in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: 22 proteins were significantly downregulated by oncogenic KRASG12V.
source: In total, we identified 17 proteins that were significantly upregulated, and 22 that were significantly downregulated (fold-change >±1.75; p-value<0.01) (Figure 1B; The full dataset can be found in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Proteins significantly altered by KRASG12V showed significant enrichment for proteins involved in cell adhesion, cell motion, and cell-cell adhesion.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of these significantly altered proteins in our datasets revealed significant enrichment for proteins involved in cell adhesion, cell motion, and cell-cell adhesion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: 13 of the proteins significantly altered by KRASG12V signaling were reversibly influenced by MEKi in the KRASG12V cells.
source: Remarkably, 13 of the proteins that were significantly altered by KRASG12V signaling were reversibly influenced by MEKi in the KRASG12V cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Very few significant changes were observed when KRASG12V cells were treated with AKTi or EGFRi.
source: By contrast, when the KRASG12V cells were treated with AKTi or EGFRi, very few significant changes were observed (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F; Full datasets can be found in Supplementary file 3 for AKTi and Supplementary file 4 for EGFRi).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F

claim: The MAPK pathway is the dominant pathway by which RAS mediates influence on the surfaceome in the MCF10A model.
source: Consistent with previous reports, our findings indicate that the MAPK pathway is the dominant pathway by which RAS mediates influence on the surfaceome in the MCF10A model.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing effects of MEKi, AKTi, and EGFRi on surface proteome

claim: The correlation between expression level changes observed in the SILAC proteomic data with those from RNAseq data was modest but significant (R2 = 0.422).
source: The correlation between expression level changes observed in the SILAC proteomic data with those from RNAseq data (Figure 1F; The full RNAseq dataset can be found in Supplementary file 5.) was modest but significant (R2 = 0.422).
evidence: Supported by comparison of SILAC and RNAseq data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Recombinant monoclonal antibodies are not commercially available for the vast majority of cell surface proteins.
source: Unfortunately, recombinant monoclonal antibodies are not commercially available for the vast majority of cell surface proteins (Wollscheid et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wollscheid et al., 2009

claim: Up to half of all commercially available antibodies are unreliable.
source: Moreover, others have shown that up to half of all commercially available antibodies are unreliable (Baker, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baker, 2015

claim: Seven high-confidence KRAS-induced single-pass transmembrane receptors were chosen for recombinant antibody engineering.
source: We leveraged the quantitative proteomic and RNAseq data to manually choose seven high-confidence KRAS-induced single-pass transmembrane receptors to advance to a recombinant antibody engineering campaign.
evidence: Supported by experimental design based on proteomic and RNAseq data

claim: All seven antibody target candidates were at least 2-fold upregulated by mass spectrometry in the KRASG12V cells as compared to empty vector.
source: All candidates were at least 2-fold upregulated as observed by mass spectrometry in the KRASG12V cells as compared to empty vector.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data

claim: CDCP1, ICAM1, and ITGB5 all play roles in cell adhesion and migration.
source: For example, CDCP1, ICAM1, and ITGB5 all play roles in cell adhesion and migration (Huttenlocher and Horwitz, 2011; Kevil et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citations to Huttenlocher and Horwitz, 2011 and Kevil et al., 2004

claim: NT5E is a nucleotidase that contributes to immune cell evasion.
source: NT5E is a nucleotidase that contributes to immune cell evasion (Antonioli et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Antonioli et al., 2016

claim: LTBR is a cytokine receptor involved in maintenance of lymphoid microenvironments.
source: LTBR is a cytokine receptor involved in maintenance of lymphoid microenvrionments (Lukashev et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lukashev et al., 2006

claim: CD55 is a complement system inhibitor.
source: CD55 is a complement system inhibitor (Sun et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 1999

claim: ANPEP is a protease thought important for metastasis.
source: ANPEP is a protease thought important for metastasis (Sørensen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sørensen et al., 2013

claim: Selections resulted in the identification of 116 unique antigen-binding sequences against the seven ECD-Fc fusion targets.
source: Selections resulted in the identification of 116 unique antigen-binding sequences against the seven ECD-Fc fusion targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: None of the antibody clones demonstrated appreciable binding to the Fc-domains fused to the antigen.
source: None of these clones demonstrated appreciable binding to the Fc-domains fused to the antigen, a testimony to the efficiency of the catch-and-release strategy.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from phage ELISA

claim: All seven proteins showed elevated expression on the MCF10A KRASG12V cells relative to the empty vector control by flow cytometry.
source: Gratifyingly, all seven proteins showed elevated expression on the MCF10A KRASG12V cells relative to the empty vector control (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A

claim: The flow cytometry data generated with the Fabs generally correlated well with the proteomic measurements.
source: Moreover, the flow cytometry data generated with the Fabs generally correlated well with the proteomic measurements.
evidence: Supported by comparison of flow cytometry and proteomic data

claim: Five of the seven targets (CDCP1, CD55 NT5E, ICAM1 and LTBR) showed high levels of expression in at least half of the eight cancer cell lines tested.
source: For five of the seven targets (CDCP1, CD55 NT5E, ICAM1 and LTBR) we observed high levels of expression in at least half of the eight cancer cell lines.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry profiling of cancer cell lines

claim: CDCP1 was ubiquitously abundant in expression across the entire panel of cancer cell lines tested.
source: Most strikingly we observed that one protein, CDCP1, was ubiquitously abundant in expression across the entire panel.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry profiling of cancer cell lines

claim: ANPEP and ITGA5 showed little detectable expression in all cancer cell lines tested.
source: In contrast, two of the proteins, ANPEP and ITGA5, showed little detectable expression in all cases.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry profiling of cancer cell lines

claim: Most of the proteins (CD55, NT5E, CDCP1, and ICAM1) had expression levels that were affected by KRAS pathway perturbation.
source: Indeed, most of these proteins (CD55, NT5E, CDCP1, and ICAM1) had expression levels that were affected by KRAS pathway perturbation, while inhibition upstream of KRAS by EGFRi had little effect in most cases (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D

claim: AKTi inhibition caused increased expression of CDCP1, NT5E, and CD55 in multiple cases.
source: Interestingly, AKTi inhibition caused increased expression of CDCP1, NT5E, and CD55 in multiple cases.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data

claim: MEK inhibition resulted in highly decreased CDCP1 expression levels in nearly every cell line tested.
source: Also notable was that MEK inhibition resulted in highly decreased CDCP1 expression levels in nearly every cell line tested.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data

claim: MAPK signaling drives both CDCP1 expression and cell-surface localization.
source: We further validated this result by western blot, demonstrating that MAPK signaling drives both CDCP1 expression and cell-surface localization (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E

claim: More than fifty genes caused a significant reduction in growth rate in the KRASG12V cells grown without growth factor when knocked down by CRISPRi.
source: Remarkably, individual knockdown of more than fifty genes caused a significant reduction (phenotype<-1 and p-value<0.05) in growth rate in the KRASG12V cells grown without growth factor, while only four genes caused a significant growth advantage when knocked down (Figure 4B; The full datasets for all three screening conditions can be found in Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Supported by CRISPRi screening data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Only four genes caused a significant growth advantage when knocked down in KRASG12V cells grown without growth factor.
source: Remarkably, individual knockdown of more than fifty genes caused a significant reduction (phenotype<-1 and p-value<0.05) in growth rate in the KRASG12V cells grown without growth factor, while only four genes caused a significant growth advantage when knocked down (Figure 4B; The full datasets for all three screening conditions can be found in Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Supported by CRISPRi screening data shown in Figure 4B

claim: There were only 12 genes in the wild type MCF10A cells that showed a growth disadvantage when knocked down.
source: Interestingly, there were only 12 genes in the wild type MCF10A cells and eight genes in the KRASG12V cells grown with growth factor that showed a growth disadvantage, and none that were increased.
evidence: Supported by CRISPRi screening data

claim: There were eight genes in the KRASG12V cells grown with growth factor that showed a growth disadvantage when knocked down.
source: Interestingly, there were only 12 genes in the wild type MCF10A cells and eight genes in the KRASG12V cells grown with growth factor that showed a growth disadvantage, and none that were increased.
evidence: Supported by CRISPRi screening data

claim: EGFR was critical for growth of wild type MCF10A grown in the presence of EGF.
source: Not surprisingly, EGFR was critical for growth of wild type MCF10A grown in the presence of EGF.
evidence: Supported by CRISPRi screening data

claim: EGFR was not critical to the KRASG12V cells grown either in the presence or absence of growth factors.
source: However, it was not critical to the KRASG12V cells grown either in the presence or absence of growth factors, which reflects the fact that constitutively active KRASG12V can drive the growth of these cells independent of EGFR signaling.
evidence: Supported by CRISPRi screening data

claim: The KRASG12V cells showed a strong dependence on proteins within the MAPK signaling pathway (RAF/MEK/ERK).
source: Furthermore, the KRASG12V cells showed a strong dependence on proteins within the MAPK signaling pathway (RAF/MEK/ERK) and little to no dependence on the PI3K/AKT pathway, consistent with previous reports highlighting the importance of RAS-driven MAPK signaling (Roberts and Der, 2007).
evidence: Supported by CRISPRi screening data and citation to Roberts and Der, 2007

claim: The KRASG12V cells showed little to no dependence on the PI3K/AKT pathway.
source: Furthermore, the KRASG12V cells showed a strong dependence on proteins within the MAPK signaling pathway (RAF/MEK/ERK) and little to no dependence on the PI3K/AKT pathway, consistent with previous reports highlighting the importance of RAS-driven MAPK signaling (Roberts and Der, 2007).
evidence: Supported by CRISPRi screening data and citation to Roberts and Der, 2007

claim: RALGDS was of intermediate importance relative to MAPK and PI3K in KRASG12V cells.
source: Interestingly, RALGDS, a lesser-studied RAS effector protein, was of intermediate importance relative to MAPK and PI3K.
evidence: Supported by CRISPRi screening data

claim: Genes critical for the growth factor independent proliferation of KRASG12V cells but unimportant for the growth of wild type cells fell into two main categories: integrin-mediated cell adhesion and Wnt signaling.
source: The set of genes that are critical for the growth factor independent proliferation of KRASG12V cells but unimportant for the growth of wild type cells notably fell into two main categories (Figure 4C). One group constitutes core components of integrin-mediated cell adhesion, while the other included major proteins involved in Wnt signaling.
evidence: Supported by CRISPRi screening data shown in Figure 4C

claim: There was very little overlap for proteins upregulated by KRAS as measured by mass spectrometry and those showing synthetic growth reduction with KRAS in the CRISPRi screen.
source: Remarkably, there was very little overlap for proteins upregulated by KRAS as measured by mass spectrometry, and those showing synthetic growth reduction with KRAS in the CRISPRi screen (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by comparison of mass spectrometry and CRISPRi data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Two genes were identified as hits in both the mass spectrometry and CRISPRi experiments: ITGB5 and CDCP1.
source: However, two genes were identified as hits in both experiments, ITGB5 and CDCP1.
evidence: Supported by comparison of mass spectrometry and CRISPRi data

claim: CDCP1 has been previously implicated as an elevated marker in solid cancers and a driver of cancer cell growth, metastasis, and tumor progression.
source: CDCP1 has been previously implicated as an elevated marker in solid cancers and a driver of cancer cell growth, metastasis, and tumor progression (Ikeda et al., 2009; Leroy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ikeda et al., 2009 and Leroy et al., 2015

claim: CDCP1 signaling can be mediated by interactions with integrins.
source: Interestingly, several groups have demonstrated that CDCP1 signaling can be mediated by interactions with integrins (Casar et al., 2014; Wright et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Casar et al., 2014 and Wright et al., 2016

claim: CDCP1 knockdown by individual sgRNA resulted in approximately 40% reduction in growth over 15 days of KRASG12V cells.
source: Using an individual sgRNA to CDCP1, we observed a ~40% reduction in growth over 15 days of KRASG12V cells with CDCP1 knocked down (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by competitive growth assay data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Oncogenic KRAS is nearly ubiquitously expressed in pancreatic cancers.
source: Oncogenic KRAS is nearly ubiquitously expressed in pancreatic cancers and these cancers are particularly dependent on MAPK pathway signaling (Eser et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eser et al., 2014

claim: Pancreatic cancers are particularly dependent on MAPK pathway signaling.
source: Oncogenic KRAS is nearly ubiquitously expressed in pancreatic cancers and these cancers are particularly dependent on MAPK pathway signaling (Eser et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eser et al., 2014

claim: CDCP1 showed high level of expression on a panel of human Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Cancer (PDAC) cell lines relative to no observable expression on non-tumorigenic pancreatic duct cells, HPNE.
source: Thus, we profiled CDCP1 expression levels on a panel of human Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Cancer (PDAC) cell lines, and observed a high level of expression of CDCP1 relative to no observable expression on non-tumorigenic pancreatic duct cells, HPNE (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A

claim: HPAC PDAC cells express approximately 2.9 million copies of CDCP1 per cell.
source: Indeed, quantification of the protein copy number of CDCP1 on the HPAC PDAC cells revealed that these cells were expressing ~2.9 million copies per cell (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: Cells containing oncogenic RAS are very active in protein uptake by macropinocytosis and lysosomal degradation.
source: Moreover, cells containing oncogenic RAS are known to be very active in protein uptake by macropinocytosis and lysosomal degradation (Commisso et al., 2013), making an ADC strategy even more attractive.
evidence: Supported by citation to Commisso et al., 2013

claim: Normal HPNE cells were unaffected by treatment of up to 20 nM of CDCP1 antibody-drug conjugate.
source: We found that while the normal HPNE cells were unaffected by treatment of up to 20 nM of antibody complex, oncogenic KRAS containing HPAC cells were sensitive to ADC treatment at concentrations as low as 10pM. (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by cell killing assay data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Oncogenic KRAS containing HPAC cells were sensitive to CDCP1 ADC treatment at concentrations as low as 10pM.
source: We found that while the normal HPNE cells were unaffected by treatment of up to 20 nM of antibody complex, oncogenic KRAS containing HPAC cells were sensitive to ADC treatment at concentrations as low as 10pM. (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by cell killing assay data shown in Figure 5C

claim: More than 60% reduction of viability was observed at 0.8 nM CDCP1 ADC treatment in HPAC cells.
source: More than 60% reduction of viability was observed at 0.8 nM (Figure 5D), suggesting that the CDCP1-selective antibody can selectively internalize and deliver the cytotoxic payload.
evidence: Supported by cell killing assay data shown in Figure 5D

claim: 1 nM of the CDCP1 BiTE was sufficient to activate 75% of T-cells when co-cultured with mutant KRAS HPAC cells.
source: Remarkably, 1 nM of the CDCP1 BiTE was sufficient to activate 75% of T-cells when co-cultured with mutant KRAS HPAC cells, while co-culture with HPNE cells, or treatment with BiTE lacking the anti-CD3 scFv, resulted in minimal activation (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by T-cell activation assay data shown in Figure 5F

claim: Co-culture with HPNE cells resulted in minimal T-cell activation with CDCP1 BiTE treatment.
source: Remarkably, 1 nM of the CDCP1 BiTE was sufficient to activate 75% of T-cells when co-cultured with mutant KRAS HPAC cells, while co-culture with HPNE cells, or treatment with BiTE lacking the anti-CD3 scFv, resulted in minimal activation (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by T-cell activation assay data shown in Figure 5F

claim: Within four hours of administration of the 89Zr-Fab, tumor localization was observed in HPAC xenograft mice.
source: Within four hours of administration of the 89Zr-Fab, tumor localization was observed, and by eight hours staining was highly pronounced (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by PET imaging data shown in Figure 5H

claim: By eight hours after administration of the 89Zr-Fab, tumor staining was highly pronounced in HPAC xenograft mice.
source: Within four hours of administration of the 89Zr-Fab, tumor localization was observed, and by eight hours staining was highly pronounced (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by PET imaging data shown in Figure 5H

claim: Significantly reduced tumor staining was observed using heat denatured 89Zr-Fab in HPAC xenograft mice.
source: Significantly reduced tumor staining was observed using the heat denatured 89Zr-Fab.
evidence: Supported by PET imaging data

claim: In HPAC xenograft mice treated with subtoxic MEKi, 89Zr-Fab tumor localization was highly diminished.
source: Strikingly, in the HPAC xenograft mice treated with subtoxic MEKi, 89Zr-Fab tumor localization was also highly diminished.
evidence: Supported by PET imaging data

claim: CDCP1 expression is a direct consequence of RAS dependent MAPK signaling even in the complex milieu of a tumor.
source: These animal data provide further evidence to the hypothesis that CDCP1 expression is a direct consequence of RAS dependent MAPK signaling even in the complex milieu of a tumor.
evidence: Supported by in vivo PET imaging data showing MEKi reduces CDCP1 expression

claim: RAS signaling can coordinately regulate a network of surface proteins in order to drive malignant hallmarks such as loss of adhesion, cell migration, and cell growth.
source: Our results suggest that RAS signaling can coordinately regulate a network of surface proteins in order to drive malignant hallmarks such as loss of adhesion, cell migration, and cell growth.
evidence: Supported by proteomic and functional data showing coordinated regulation of surface proteins

claim: Cells with oncogenic KRAS display high expression levels of several integrins (ITGB5/ITGB1/ITGA5/ITGA3) in combination with CDCP1.
source: For example, we observed that cells with oncogenic KRAS display high expression levels of several integrins (ITGB5/ITGB1/ITGA5/ITGA3) in combination with CDCP1.
evidence: Supported by proteomic data

claim: CDCP1/integrin complexes can drive AKT dependent loss of adhesion, cell growth, and anti-anoikis signaling.
source: Previous work has identified a signaling axis through which CDCP1/integrin complexes can drive AKT dependent loss of adhesion, cell growth, and anti-anoikis signaling (Casar et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Casar et al., 2014

claim: Knockdown of CDCP1 or ITGB5 slows the growth of cells addicted to RAS signaling.
source: We found that knockdown of CDCP1 or ITGB5 slows the growth of cells addicted to RAS signaling, supporting the idea that oncogenic RAS promotes the expression of these proteins to enable tumor cell growth.
evidence: Supported by CRISPRi screening data

claim: Nearly half of the proteins observed to be enriched on the surface of KRAS-transformed MCF10As were decreased in expression level when cells were treated with a MEK inhibitor.
source: Nearly half of the proteins we observed to be enriched on the surface of KRAS-transformed MCF10As were decreased in expression level when cells were treated with a MEK inhibitor.
evidence: Supported by proteomic data comparing KRAS-transformed cells with and without MEK inhibitor treatment

claim: Treatment with EGF and AKT inhibition had little consequence on the set of RAS enriched membrane proteins.
source: Conversely, treatment with EGF and AKT inhibition had little consequence on this set of RAS enriched membrane proteins.
evidence: Supported by proteomic data

claim: A subset of RAS-induced surface proteins could serve as new biomarkers for both RAS dependent MAPK signaling and drug efficacy of MAPK pathway inhibitors.
source: Furthermore, our data suggest that a subset of these proteins could serve as new biomarkers for both RAS dependent MAPK signaling and drug efficacy of MAPK pathway inhibitors.
evidence: Supported by data showing MAPK-dependent regulation of surface proteins and in vivo imaging

claim: CDCP1 expression was driven by RAS dependent MAPK signaling in more than a dozen mutant RAS cancer cell lines.
source: Our initial observation that CDCP1 expression was driven by RAS dependent MAPK signaling in MCF10As was recapitulated in more than a dozen mutant RAS cancer cell lines as well as an in vivo model for pancreatic cancer.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry profiling of cancer cell lines and in vivo imaging data

claim: CDCP1 expression was driven by RAS dependent MAPK signaling in an in vivo model for pancreatic cancer.
source: Our initial observation that CDCP1 expression was driven by RAS dependent MAPK signaling in MCF10As was recapitulated in more than a dozen mutant RAS cancer cell lines as well as an in vivo model for pancreatic cancer.
evidence: Supported by in vivo PET imaging data

claim: CDCP1 is important for proliferation in RAS-addicted cells.
source: Additionally, we show that CDCP1 is important for proliferation in RAS-addicted cells, suggesting a significant link between its function and its upregulated surface expression.
evidence: Supported by CRISPRi screening data

claim: Mutant RAS PDAC cells express nearly 3 million copies of CDCP1 per cell.
source: Additionally, we showed that mutant RAS PDAC cells express nearly 3 million copies per cell, a number comparable to the estimated 2 million copies per cell that can be observed in HER positive breast cancers.
evidence: Supported by quantification data

claim: HER positive breast cancers express an estimated 2 million copies of HER2 per cell.
source: Additionally, we showed that mutant RAS PDAC cells express nearly 3 million copies per cell, a number comparable to the estimated 2 million copies per cell that can be observed in HER positive breast cancers.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about HER2 expression

claim: CDCP1 normal tissue expression is quite restricted compared to HER2.
source: However, analysis of the GTEX tissue expression database reveals that CDCP1 normal tissue expression is quite restricted (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B). In comparison to the classical antibody-targeted cell-surface protein, HER2, normal tissue expression for CDCP1 is far lower (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by GTEX database analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and 1C

claim: KRAS-transformed cells have a selective dependence on the surfaceome to maintain both Integrin and Wnt signaling.
source: We discovered KRAS-transformed cells have a selective dependence on the surfaceome to maintain both Integrin and Wnt signaling, pathways critical for regulation of adhesion and cell migration, respectively.
evidence: Supported by CRISPRi screening data

claim: CDCP1 is a protein known to drive loss of adhesion through integrin signaling.
source: One of these targets, CUB Domain Containing Protein 1 (CDCP1), a protein known to drive loss of adhesion through integrin signaling (Bhatt et al., 2005; Casar et al., 2014), was a common hit in both our MS and CRISPRi screens.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bhatt et al., 2005 and Casar et al., 2014

claim: Recombinant antibodies to CDCP1 can be used to selectively deliver therapeutic cytotoxic payloads to pancreatic cancer cells while sparing normal control cells.
source: We focused on this example and showed that recombinant antibodies to CDCP1 can be used to selectively deliver therapeutic cytotoxic payloads or recruit and activate T-cells to pancreatic cancer cells while sparing normal control cells.
evidence: Supported by ADC and BiTE experimental data

claim: Recombinant antibodies to CDCP1 can be used to recruit and activate T-cells to pancreatic cancer cells while sparing normal control cells.
source: We focused on this example and showed that recombinant antibodies to CDCP1 can be used to selectively deliver therapeutic cytotoxic payloads or recruit and activate T-cells to pancreatic cancer cells while sparing normal control cells.
evidence: Supported by BiTE experimental data

claim: CDCP1 expression level is an abundant biomarker for RAS signaling through the MAPK signaling pathway in mouse xenograft models for pancreatic cancer.
source: We further show in mouse xenograft models for pancreatic cancer that CDCP1 expression level is an abundant biomarker for RAS signaling through the MAPK signaling pathway.
evidence: Supported by in vivo PET imaging data

claim: The diploid MCF10A cell line is non-malignant and harbors only small genetic modifications typical of a culture adapted cell line.
source: The diploid MCF10A cell line is often used for oncogenic transformation studies because it is non-malignant and harbors only small genetic modifications typical of a culture adapted cell line.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about MCF10A cells

claim: MCF10A cells are readily transduced with lentivirus.
source: In addition, MCF10As are readily transduced with lentivirus, which enabled the rapid generation of the isogenic model as well as the possibility to engineer these cells further for downstream validation studies.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about MCF10A cells

claim: RAS is rarely implicated in breast cancer.
source: While MCF10A cells are mammary in origin, and RAS is rarely implicated in breast cancer, we believe that the benefits of this model outweighs this caveat.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about RAS mutations in cancer

claim: RAS signaling in any epithelial cell type would result in a common transcriptional program and signature of cell-surface protein expression.
source: Moreover, we hypothesized RAS signaling in any epithelial cell type would result in a common transcriptional program and signature of cell-surface protein expression.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors

claim: The surfaceome changes substantially in MCF10A cells expressing oncogenic KRAS.
source: Recently, we showed using initial proteomics discovery experiments that the surfaceome does indeed change substantially in MCF10A cells expressing oncogenic KRAS (Ye et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ye et al., 2016

claim: Biological replicates for the MEKi experiment showed reasonable correlation in fold-changes in expression (R2 = 0.61).
source: Biological replicates showed similar overlap and reasonable correlation in fold-changes in expression ± MEKi (R2 = 0.61), indicating biological and technical reproducibility (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C

claim: The MAPK pathway is important for RAS-mediated transformation and tumorigenesis.
source: Others have shown the importance of the MAPK pathway for RAS-mediated transformation and tumerogenesis (Roberts and Der, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roberts and Der, 2007

claim: Overexpression of oncogenic RAS in model cell lines contributes to loss of adhesion, increased invasive properties, and evasion of immune responses.
source: Overexpression of oncogenic RAS in model cell lines contributes to loss of adhesion, increased invasive properties, and evasion of immune responses, phenotypes that depend on the function of membrane proteins (Pylayeva-Gupta et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pylayeva-Gupta et al., 2011

claim: RAS-driven transcriptional reprogramming coordinately regulates the expression of cell surface proteins to exert malignant phenotypes.
source: This suggests that RAS-driven transcriptional reprogramming coordinately regulates the expression of cell surface proteins to exert malignant phenotypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that RAS affects membrane protein-dependent phenotypes

claim: RAS is a family of three ubiquitously expressed small GTPases found in all animal cell types.
source: RAS is a family of three ubiquitously expressed small GTPases found in all animal cell types.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about RAS

claim: RAS is localized to the intracellular leaflet of the cell membrane.
